name: Fatima Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the van by half seven with Gary, the older electrician, and most days we're in an old terraced house pulling out wiring from the 1960s. Today it was a fuse board change and a new cooker circuit for a woman on Mill Street. I love the moment you flick the main switch back on and a whole family's house lights up because of you. What wears me out is lofts in summer, and customers who've watched one video and think they know better.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come into the trade, and who do you work for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad's a plumber, and I used to go out with him on Saturdays from when I was twelve. I did a college course, then a four-year apprenticeship with Derek Hallam, and I've been at his firm ever since. It's five of us: Derek, his daughter Kirsty in the office, Gary, me and Callum, our apprentice. I still write my job sheets on paper, which drives Kirsty up the wall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what does life look like right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I still live at my parents' place, because I'm getting married to Imran next summer and we're saving. I've got about four months of money put by, and most of it is meant for the wedding and a house deposit. Sunday lunch is at my mum's whatever happens, and I don't touch my phone at the table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. People at the wholesaler, the shop where we buy our cable, have been going on about AI for two years. Nobody's rewiring a 1930s terrace with a chatbot, and they won't be next year either. I'd say it in the van to Gary and he'd laugh, because he's been saying it longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but my worries wouldn't go anywhere. Derek's 63 and he keeps hinting about selling the firm, and I don't know who'd buy it or whether they'd keep me. Robots aren't what keeps me up, it's Derek's retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, five days on the tools and the odd Saturday call-out. I'd keep putting a set amount into the house fund every payday, because Imran and I want a deposit within three years of the wedding. And I'd ask Derek straight out what his plans are, over a tea in the yard, instead of guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, a bit smug if I'm honest. But there's a knot about Derek that doesn't go away just because the computers stayed dumb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Derek might sell. If he did, what would you do that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring round the other small firms in town first, the ones I know from the wholesaler counter. There's two or three that are always short of a qualified electrician, so I wouldn't starve. What I'd hate is going to one of the big outfits with an app that tracks every minute you spend on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI would automate some routine tasks. Does any of that touch your own day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kirsty does the invoices and the bookings, so maybe her job changes, not mine. She tried to get us on a job app last year and I kept writing my sheets on paper till she gave up. My hands still have to strip the cable and test the circuit, and no software does that.

say: I'd say **AI was hype** and nobody rewires an old terrace with a chatbot.
I'd make the point in the van to **Gary**, who's said it for years.
I'd tell people at the **wholesaler counter** that the trade carries on as before.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, because my hands-on work was never really at risk.
My real worry is **Derek selling** the firm and whether a new owner keeps me.
Any routine automation lands on **Kirsty's office work**, not on my rewires.
do: Keep working **five days** on rewires, plus the odd Saturday call-out.
Pay a set amount into the **house fund** every payday for a deposit within three years.
Ask Derek **straight out** about his retirement plans over a tea in the yard.
feel: Mostly **settled**, even a bit smug that the hype came to nothing.
Still a **knot of worry** about Derek's firm that AI has nothing to do with.
S0.quote: Nobody's rewiring a 1930s terrace with a chatbot, and they won't be next year either.
fieldNote: Her steadiest worry is **Derek's age** and a possible sale, not technology at all.
She resisted the firm's **job app** and still writes paper job sheets on purpose.
She is confident she'd **find work** at another small firm, but dreads big, app-run outfits.

steps.text: Keep doing rewires and fuse board changes at Derek's firm
Pay a set amount into the house deposit fund every payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the office people, but my job's safe. Someone still has to crawl under the floorboards of an old house and find where the last bloke joined the cable with tape. I'd say that loud at the wholesaler counter, and most of the lads would agree with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it hits Kirsty's job and the quoting first, and then Derek decides he can run the firm with fewer people. If customers get quotes off some website in ten seconds, the cheaper firms win and Derek can't compete on price. So the work stays, but little firms like ours get squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working, and I'd save harder, maybe an extra few hours of overtime a month into the house fund. I wouldn't go on any AI course, I'll tell you that now. I'd wait and see what Derek does before I jumped anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. My hands are fine, but the ground under the firm feels a bit soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kirsty, first, because bookings and invoices are exactly what you're describing. And Callum, our apprentice, who's 19 and only halfway through. If my boss Derek cuts back, the apprentice is the easiest saving, and that's wrong, because apprenticeships are how this trade carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never go on an AI course. What if Derek asked you to use a quoting app on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grumble, and then I'd probably do it, because he pays my wages. But I'd keep my paper sheets in the van as a backup, because apps crash and paper doesn't. Gary would do the same, he's worse than me.

say: I'd say my job is **safe** because someone still has to get under the floorboards.
I'd tell the **office people** good luck, since their work is what changes.
think: I expect **quoting and bookings** to move to software first, starting with Kirsty's job.
Cheap online quotes could **squeeze small firms** like Derek's on price.
The **work stays**, but fewer people might share it at our firm.
do: Work **extra overtime** each month and put it into the house fund.
Refuse any **AI course**, though she'd use an app if Derek insisted.
**Wait** to see whether Derek cuts staff before looking elsewhere.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the firm feels shaky even though her hands-on work is fine.
S1.quote: If my boss Derek cuts back, the apprentice is the easiest saving, and that's wrong, because apprenticeships are how this trade carries on.
fieldNote: She worries first for **Callum and Kirsty**, not herself, which shows loyalty to the small firm.
Her **apprenticeship values** come through strongly: the trade is passed on by hand.
She says she'd never learn AI, then admits she'd **comply** if her boss asked.

steps.text: Keep doing rewires and repairs at Derek's firm as normal
Work extra overtime hours and pay them into the house fund
Wait to see whether Derek cuts staff before looking elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and that the government should have stopped it. You don't let a few tech companies rip up everybody's living in two years. At the wedding I'd be telling my uncles it's the end of proper work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I think the first two years I'm fine, because the paperwork side goes but my hands don't. It's 2031 that frightens me. I'd be 32, married, maybe with a baby on the way, and a robot that can wire a house as well as me would finish small firms like Derek's for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop spending on anything that isn't the wedding or the house fund: no new tools, no holiday. I'd talk to Imran about pushing the house back and staying at my parents' longer, to keep cash. And I'd lean on family, my dad's always said we look after our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. And angry. I did everything right, the apprenticeship, the licence, and it feels like the rules changed after I'd played.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be 32 when the robots come. What would you tell Imran that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we can't count on my wage after 2031, so we plan as if his job is the main one. That's hard for me to say, I've always paid my way. But Imran works in a warehouse office doing the stock orders, and if the thinking AI gets there first, his job's not safe either, so honestly I don't know what we'd plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never do an AI course. With three years before the robots arrive, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know how that sounds. What would I even learn, to manage the robot that took my job? I'd rather spend those three years earning everything I can on the tools and putting it away, every overtime shift Derek offers.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and the government should have **stopped it**.
I'd tell my uncles at the wedding it's the **end of proper work**.
think: The first two years feel fine, because only the **paperwork** side goes.
**2031** is the real fear, when robots could wire a house as well as she can.
Small firms like **Derek's** would be finished for good once robots arrive.
do: Cut all spending except the **wedding** and the **house fund**.
Push the **house purchase** back and stay at her parents' longer.
Take **every overtime shift** until 2031 and bank the money.
feel: **Scared**, picturing herself at 32 without a trade.
**Angry** that she followed every rule and the rules changed anyway.
S2.quote: I did everything right, the apprenticeship, the licence, and it feels like the rules changed after I'd played.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year gap** clearly: paperwork goes first, her hands later.
Both incomes look **exposed**: Imran's stock-ordering job meets thinking AI in 2028.
She refuses to **retrain** even with warning, and banks money instead.
Her fallback is **family support**, which fits her traditional view of looking after your own.

steps.text: Stop buying new tools and cancel this year's holiday
Delay buying a house and live at her parents' longer
Take every overtime shift Derek offers until 2031 and bank it
Ask her dad and wider family for help if her wage stops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before, that somebody should put the brakes on. But I'd add that at least there's time for the government to sort out training and support for trades. People round me would want to hear something practical, not just moaning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but not as much better as it sounds. Robots by 2034 means I'm 35, maybe with a kid at nursery. Five years buys me more money in the bank, not more safety in my trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married next summer, nothing changes there. Then I'd save hard and try to pay off as much of a small mortgage as we can before 2034. I'd probably join the electricians' trade association too, so somebody's speaking up for small firms and apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not in a panic. There's a plan, even if it's a plain one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight before the robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, and the gym I never go to anyway. Then I'd sell my car and share Imran's, because the firm's van gets me to work. The wedding stays, my mum would never forgive me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier small firms get squeezed. With five years' warning, does Derek's firm survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Derek retires before 2031, I'm sure of that now. Maybe Gary and I could buy the van and the customer list off him, but I'm not a business person and that scares me. More likely I go to another small firm and hope they last.

say: I'd still say someone should **put the brakes on**.
I'd add that there's **time** for the government to support the trades properly.
think: Robots by **2034** mean she is 35, maybe with a young child.
Five years gives her **more savings**, but not more safety in her trade.
Derek will **retire** before then, so she'll likely move to another small firm.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** next summer as planned.
Overpay a **small mortgage** as hard as possible before 2034.
Join the electricians' **trade association** to speak up for small firms and apprentices.
feel: **Worried** but not panicking, because she has a plain plan.
S3.quote: Five years buys me more money in the bank, not more safety in my trade.
fieldNote: She treats the extra time as **earning time**, not time to change course.
She still expects her **trade to shrink** by 2034, so the threat is real but further off.
Buying Derek's firm tempts her, but she says **business scares her**.
Joining a **trade association** is her first ever step into group action.

steps.text: Overpay the mortgage as much as possible before 2034
Sell her own car and share Imran's to cut costs
Join the electricians' trade association to speak up for apprentices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can change, governments can step in. I'd tell people not to panic, keep working and keep training youngsters properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years gets me to 37 before AGI and about 40 before the robots. That's most of my working life on the tools, and I'd be lying if I said that didn't feel a lot better. But I'd still be finishing my career early, and I don't know doing what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the firm and keep saving like I do now. I'd vote for whoever promises to protect apprenticeships and trades, and I'd actually write to our local representative, which I've never done. Maybe later I'd look at the inspection and testing qualification, but not straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier, much easier. There's still a cloud on the horizon, but it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the inspection and testing qualification. What is it, and why not straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a qualification to test and certify other people's wiring, so you sign off that a job is safe. I'd want to see first whether robots' work even needs a person to sign it off. If it does, I'd do the course around 2035, no point paying for it early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years covers your late twenties and most of your thirties. Does it change your family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me want kids sooner, if anything, while my wage is steady. My mum had me at 26 and she says the early years are when you've got the energy. If the robots come around 2039, I'd want our kids at school and the house mostly paid off by then.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long enough for governments to step in.
I'd tell people **not to panic** and to keep training youngsters properly.
think: Robots around **2039** leave her most of her working life on the tools.
She still expects to **finish her career early**, with no idea what comes after.
do: Keep working at **Derek's firm** and saving at the same rate.
Write to the **local representative** about protecting apprenticeships, a first for her.
Try for **children sooner** while her wage is steady.
feel: A distant **cloud** remains about how her career ends.
S4.quote: If the robots come around 2039, I'd want our kids at school and the house mostly paid off by then.
fieldNote: The decade turns her plans toward **family timing** rather than any career change.
She holds off **retraining** until she sees whether robot work needs human sign-off.
Her answer to change is **politics**: protecting apprenticeships, not public handouts.

steps.text: Keep wiring houses at Derek's firm and helping train Callum
Keep the set monthly payment into the house fund going
Write to the local representative about protecting apprenticeships
Try for children sooner while her wage is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. The robots would turn up when I'm 32, just married, with no house bought and maybe a baby. What would help is support for trades people, not handouts: help with the mortgage while you change trade, and rules that make companies keep apprentices on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Derek selling the firm, and honestly that worries me more today than any robot. A good small firm is like a family, and when the owner retires it can just vanish. Somebody should help the workers buy those firms instead of letting them close.

headlineQuote: I love the moment you flick the main switch back on and a whole family's house lights up because of you.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old electrician** at a five-person family firm, rewiring old terraced houses.
She is engaged to **Imran**, lives with her parents and saves about **four months** of money.
She distrusts apps and **refuses AI courses**, and still writes job sheets on paper.
Her steady worry is **Derek retiring**; the fast AGI picture makes her alarmed about 2031.
With more warning she **banks money**, joins a trade association and plans children sooner.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would arrive when she is 32 and newly married.
Her boss **Derek retiring** and the firm vanishing worries her more today than any robot.
whatWouldHelp: **Mortgage help** while trades people change work, rather than handouts.
Rules that make firms **keep apprentices**, and help for workers to **buy** small firms.
